title: Give to the pot, or keep it?
hook: Every dollar in the pot turns into $3 for the street. So why would anyone hold back?

knows: a shared project can benefit everyone
doesNotKnow: why people hold back when a shared good benefits everyone
that what pays for one person can differ from what pays for the group

misconception: If a shared project is worth it for the group, people will pay for it.
objective: The learner can explain that when each dollar given returns less than a dollar to the giver, holding back pays for each person even though giving pays for the group.

claims.text: With 10 neighbours holding $10 each and every pot dollar becoming $3 shared equally, if you give all $10 and the others give nothing, you end with $3 and each of them with $13.
claims.source: Pot 10 × 3 = 30; share 30 / 10 = 3. You: 0 + 3 = 3. Others: 10 + 3 = 13. Demo.tsx payoffs().

claims.text: In that case the group goes from $100 to $120.
claims.source: 3 + 9 × 13 = 120. (The brief's key state said $130; recomputed as $120.)

claims.text: If everyone gives $10, everyone ends with $30.
Each dollar you give returns 30 cents to you, so whatever the others do, each dollar held back leaves you 70 cents better off while the group loses $2.
claims.source: Your total = 10 − g + 0.3 × (g + others) has slope −0.7 in g; group total = 100 + 2 × pot. (The brief said $2.70 per dollar; recomputed as $0.70.)

claims.text: The 'some' setting is one seeded draw of the nine neighbours' gifts ($0 to $10 each).
claims.source: mulberry32 seed 7, untuned (first seed tried): gifts 0, 0, 10, 7, 5, 4, 5, 2, 6 (sum 39). It illustrates c4; c4 does not rest on it.

claims.text: The lesson is a model of one round with no talking and no punishment; in lab versions of this game many people do give, at least at first.
claims.source: J. O. Ledyard (1995), 'Public Goods: A Survey of Experimental Research', in Kagel & Roth (eds.), Handbook of Experimental Economics: one-shot and early-round contributions typically 40–60% of the endowment, falling with repetition.

recall.question: Five flatmates share a cleaning fund. Each $1 put in buys $2 of cleaning that all five share equally. For one flatmate, what does each $1 they put in bring back to them?
recall.why: $1 becomes $2 of benefit split five ways, so the giver gets 40 cents of it. For each person holding back pays; for the group giving pays.
